utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. I think we are continuing with the witness Janc, with the cross-examination, and therefore the -- would you like to raise something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The witness can come in. I just wanted to raise something, just to bring it to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you and to Your Honours. Mr. President, we've had an opportunity to review the audiotape of Mr. Erdemovic's testimony in the Popovic case, and it appears that there was a mistranslation of a term that he used. The used the term "vodnik" to describe his position in the 10th Sabotage Unit, which was translated erroneously "corporal." It should have been "sergeant," that would have been the more appropriate translation. So I wanted to alert you to the fact that we would be making the application to correct that in that transcript, and I believe since it was read in in this case, we would have to move also to have it corrected in this case as well. But that's all I wanted to let you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back to this courtroom. I would like to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir has some questions for you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we are not receiving the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English now? Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. Please, Mr. Tolimir, repeat what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May there be peace in this house for all those present, and may God's will be done in these proceedings, and may the outcome be as God wishes and not as I wish. I'd like to say good afternoon to Mr. Janc and thank him for coming in again. I have a few questions to ask Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Janc, you spoke about a list compiled by the International Commission on Missing Persons, the ICMP. My first question is: Can you tell us a little more about the list was compiled or, rather, the methodology in compiling the list? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to do so, although I think that would be the question for the ICMP itself. But I think that we have gone over this -- over this -- their methodology during my previous testimonies. So, basically, what they are doing is they are getting the DNA samples, which are taken out of the bodies or body remains during the autopsies, and these samples are then sent to their office in Sarajevo. After that, these samples are tested and a DNA profile is established and then matched to a donor. It means that the person is identified, I mean, the person which is on the missing list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. You also spoke about a list compiled by the International Commission. Well, I'm going to ask you the same question, because I can't ask the representatives of the International Commission how they compiled the list, so I'm asking you, because you used their list as a basis for some of your conclusions and some of the things you presented here. So let me repeat. There is a list compiled by the International Commission on Missing Persons, and there's also a list of missing persons compiled by the International Red Cross Committee. Can you tell us, first of all, what the methodology was used for the missing persons list of the ICRC, led by the ICRC, the International Red Cross? And then we'll come to the next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Regarding the ICRC, my response would be the same, so that the representatives from those institutions would be the best people to respond. But, in any case, I know that the relatives reported the -- their loved ones which went missing after the fall of Srebrenica, and that this process was ongoing process in Bosnia up until the -- recently, I think, that we don't have the ICRC office anymore in Sarajevo, if I'm not mistaken. So this list was compiled first after the fall of Srebrenica, and it was updated on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, can you tell me this: What is the relationship between the two lists, or, rather, are there any differences with respect to the number of missing persons, the errors in names, the dates of birth, or any other facts like that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those two lists are different. For example, on the ICRC list, you will find much more exact information regarding when and where the individual went missing; whereas on the ICMP list, this information for most of the individuals would be 11 of July. And I think these are two unrelated lists, actually, because ICMP has their own database on the donors, of the relatives which individuals went missing after the fall of Srebrenica, so they have compiled their own database based on the donors for these relatives. So these are two different lists, and what I have been mostly relying into my report for calculating the total numbers was the ICMP list.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You need the microphone, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. You said a moment ago that that list was about individuals that disappeared on the 11th of July. Now, can it then be valid in the analyses that we are considering here in court? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant by "11 of July" is that you can find on the ICMP list, as a date of disappearance, 11 of July, but that was just their decision to put it like that, that they went missing on 11 of July, basically, because for their purposes that would mean that this is Srebrenica-related missing person. They did not go into details, when and where exactly such particular individual went missing. So in order to find this information, we are -- we are consulting the ICRC missing list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does that mean that in this list, you can have somebody who disappeared in 1992, or 1993, or 1994, or 1995, and that they are, in fact, being listed as having gone missing in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't mean that. You don't have such individuals on that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But you said a moment ago, in your previous answer, that they list everybody as having disappeared on the 11th of July, 1995; is that correct or have I misunderstood? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not everybody, but for most of the people -- for most of them, will you find the entry as went missing on 11 of July. But what I mean for most of them, I mean on the ICMP list which is related only to Srebrenica event. So not everybody for which they have information that everybody disappeared in Bosnia would be missing from 11 of July. For example, if the person went missing before from some other incident, those individuals would not be included into the list which I used for my report, so those would be part of the other ICMP lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, if somebody from Srebrenica disappeared in 1992 or 1993, and if there are facts about that, and witnesses, and knowledge, and documents to bear that out, and that person is on that missing persons list, then would the ICRC have that person's name on its list as a missing person? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the correct answer would be, no, those people should not be on such list as being related to Srebrenica events. So if there is information on those individual, that they went missing from -- at some other point in time, not related to Srebrenica, most probably those information would reflect that on both lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you come by information of that kind, and you've just told us that those lists list the persons missing as of the 11th of July, what do you do to actually establish when the people went missing and how, or do you just ascribe it all to missing in Srebrenica in 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we don't do it like that. All the people which are on the Srebrenica missing list -- ICRC Srebrenica missing list have been checked methodological by our Demographic Unit, so the Demographic Unit checked the names on those lists against the available sources, like as it is voters lists and then census list, and in order to identify that -- in order to establish that these persons, indeed, lived at that time in Bosnia. So it is a process which have been done by the OTP, mostly by the Demographic Unit, in order to confirm that, indeed, all the individual which are on those lists are related to Srebrenica events. And if at any time there was any doubt about it, so we have double-check it, and there were several requests for assistance sent to Bosnia. We have been interviewing the individuals from certain institutions. And also if there were individuals, and I can tell you there were only -- not many of them found on those lists which, indeed, have not been related to Srebrenica, they were then excluded from these lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. I'd now like to remind you of something you said on the 13th of May, 2010, in this same trial, when you were here first. You say, on 1760 of the transcript, lines 14 to 17, the following, and I quote: "In the aim of collecting information about the dates of -- the dates when persons disappeared, we have to look at various sources, such as the ICRC missing persons list and the missing persons list of the Prosecutor's Office." Did I understand you correctly? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, that's exactly what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, since you said that, can you tell us anything about the Prosecutor's list of missing persons, the OTP's list, because we have investigators here, so can you tell us whether that list, the OTP's list, has been disclosed, perhaps under another title, or heading, or name, or whatever? I don't know how it is listed and stored in the Prosecutor's Office. But could you tell us something about that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. And this list will be actually presented by the upcoming witness, demographic expert, Helge Brunborg, who compiled that OTP list, and I think he will be the best person to explain how, exactly, it was compiled, for what purposes. And I think this list -- this list has been disclosed to you, for sure, together with his document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to remind you of that, and of something you said further on, as well, when you referred to the International Commission's missing persons list. You said, and I quote: "In most cases, most of the entries and dates for the missing persons is the 11th of July, because the purpose of their database was not to establish when and where those individuals disappeared, but what was most important for them was to establish that they were linked to Srebrenica in one way or another. So that for most of them, they put the date being the 11th of July." Did I quote you correctly, and can you remember having said that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember having said that, and you quoted me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then can I ask you this, and I'd like to hear your answer: How does the International Commission for Missing Persons -- how is it able to establish whether somebody who disappeared was linked to Srebrenica if they don't have the information about when they disappeared, whether they were members of the army, and similar facts? Thank you -- and where they disappeared, in actual fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I already testified that the exact methodology how they have done this process, I'm not aware of, but I'm not saying that they did not have in their possession any other lists in order to prove certain facts. So how was that done exactly, I don't know, by their side, but I think that they have had in their possession the actual ICRC list in order to find the donors for the missing individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, am I right in saying, on the basis of what you've just told us -- or, rather, let me ask you this: How does the International Commission establish that somebody was linked to the events in Srebrenica? Did you investigate that, since you used their lists, and particularly in view of the fact that they stipulated the date, which was the 11th of July, and some people might have gone missing before that date in Srebrenica, for instance?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say they basically referred to the ICRC missing list, but we haven't investigated -- me, in particular, I haven't investigated this issue in big depth because I know it was investigated by the Demographic Unit, itself, and they will know all these answers in -- during their testimony. So I just know some general -- general information on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Since you said that they had a choice, the ICRC list, now why did they omit from that source data about the day, place, and manner in which the person went missing, and why they put a sweeping date of the 11th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the answer on this question. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, before you we heard testimony from Mr. Ruez, an OTP investigator, and he said that he considers all those who were buried were the victims of execution. Can I hear your stand on that? Do you consider that all the people buried -- the bodies buried in mass graves were, in fact, victims deprived of their life against the law? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my position on this topic is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you repeat it for us, please, for the transcript? Repeat your position, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position would be the same as Mr. Ruez's, that the people buried at primary and secondary mass -- inside these mass graves are, indeed, the victims of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were here last time and testified, you said that in Bratunac, the grave in Bratunac, there were those who had been buried in 1992 and in 1995 as well. Does that mean that you consider them to be the victims of the conflict of 1995, and that you listed them as such?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was discussion also during my testimony here the other day, that there is a mixed grave in Bljeceva, which is very close to Bratunac. There's the secondary grave Bljeceva 1, and we know that most of the bodies there are from some other incidents from 1992, and a minority of them is from the killings -- or from the killings, yeah, which are relate to do Kravica, so they were reburied from Glogova primary grave to this site. So that's -- that's what I testified about, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. I took the example from your testimony, and by doing so I wanted to indicate that you cannot consider all these people in the graves to be victims of the events that we are discussing here and for which I am being tried. Am I right or not? Please state your views. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should be more precise. I cannot consider all these people in the graves to be victims of the events -- can you explain a little bit more, in detail, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I asked for your position earlier on, and I'll tell you what I think. Did you, as an investigator, take up a position of any kind on the basis of your opinions, or did you do that on the basis of documents, did you base your opinions on the basis of documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took up my position based on many, many things, many sources. These are documents, victim statements, then forensic evidence and such sources. So, yes, based on these sources, we have made these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, can you tell me whether you studied the lists from those aspects, the lists of the Army of Republika Srpska and the BH Army relating to the victims in armed combat, and in fighting, and in the incidents that took place in Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of those lists and I have been looking at those lists. But already the Demographic Unit concluded that these lists are not that reliable, so I did not put that much weight on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, I realise that. There is no English interpretation at the moment. Is there now interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Do you hear the English now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now we hear it again. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir, and repeat the last portion of your -- just carry on with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, we heard your answer a moment ago, and it's been recorded in the transcript. My question is this: Did you consider the document of -- a BH army document or a VRS document irrelevant that spoke of some deaths before or after the Srebrenica events that are at issue before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course not. These documents are relevant. What I've been talking about what I did not consider as relevant lists are -- I know that we received recently the list of ABiH soldiers which went missing somewhere in 1992/1993. That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. We will show here specifically such documents and the way that you have classified them. But before we move to that topic, I would like to ask you to tell us a few words about this International Commission. You said that its headquarters are in Sarajevo, and we heard from the OTP here that this is a non-government organisation, so could you please tell us something about this commission and how it was established? The International Commission of Missing Persons, that's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just in general, I know that it was established somewhere in 2001. I think it was financed by the United States government, if I'm not wrong, but I cannot be sure about that. And, yeah, their main purpose was to identify missing -- all the missing people from the conflicts which occurred in Bosnia during the war, and those identifications would be made based on the DNA analysis. So their main purpose is to identify missing persons within victims of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Am I wrong in saying that this commission may have been established in 1996, at the initiative of the president of the United States, Bill Clinton, at the G-7 meeting in Lyon in France? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything, because actually I don't know. But I know that they have started DNA identification in November 2001. But all this data about the establishment and everything is available on web site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us here, before this Trial Chamber, who directs the work of the International Commission on Missing Persons and who supervises their work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot answer this question. I know that the person who testifies here representing the ICMP is Dr. Thomas Parson. So for the rest of your question, I think I'm unable to provide you with an answer right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Do you know, by any chance, who were the chair people of this board of the International Commission on Missing Persons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I don't have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you exchanged communications with them and -- did you ever exchange information or did you just use their lists?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean me, personally, I haven't exchanged any information with them. And as you can see from the documents which are part of my report, so I am referring here to the ICMP responses, you will see that I was not involved personally in the e-mail communication with them. But I have used their lists, of course, for the purposes of my -- of my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, please, did your predecessor from whom you actually got these reports, and I mean Mr. Manning, did you get the list from him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of list do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I mean the list of missing persons and victims that you presented here by grave-site and by dates when they went missing, and established, based on DNA analysis, and based on which you also actually matched the information to the victim.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many of those information were part of his previous reports, so I have simply found this information inside his reports. And what I have been using mainly for the purposes of my report, the recent one, was the most recent information/data from the ICMP. And, yeah, so I haven't got any special data from Dean Manning, because when I joined the Tribunal he hasn't been here for many years already. So we just met, I think, two times now in life, and that's all, so I haven't got anything in particular from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long have you been in this position, from what year, could you tell us for the transcript? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the 1st of June, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, then, whether you know that as of 1996, for instance, the chairman of the board of the International Commission on Missing Persons was Cyrus Vance, and as of 1997, up until 2001, when you took over from Manning, that it was the American senator, Bob Dole, who was then succeeded by the current chairman, David Kinsey, who is now the current chairman of this commission? Am I correct in saying this? Do you have any information on that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any information on any of those names, so I cannot help you with that. So those names are not familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were stating in your question that Mr. Janc took over his duty from Mr. Manning in 2001. But as you realise the last answer of this witness, he told you that he started his work on the 1st of June, 2006. You should realise such kind of information if you put the next question to the witness. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I just asked this because the witness said that he used their list as the underlying -- as the source for his analysis that he presented here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this response was not appropriate. You said, and this is at page 14, line 24 and 25: "... up until 2001, when you took over from Manning." You can see that on this transcript. And you just before got the answer: "Yes, from the 1st of June, 2006." There's a gap of five years. This was the problem. Please carry on, and don't dispute this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like now the witness to answer my question. Who was the chairman at the time when Mr. Manning left the post that you are now occupying, and who it was in the meantime when you got appointed to your position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean -- I guess you mean the chairman of the ICMP, and I already testified that I don't have information on that. So I don't have -- I don't know, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we misunderstood each other. My question was: Who was in this post between your appointment and Manning's -- when Manning left? Who was it at that post within the OTP in the meantime? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were many investigators who have been involved investigating Srebrenica events, but in between I don't think anyone in particular was involved with the exhumations. So I think there is a gap when he left and when I took over these responsibilities, and that's why, when Dean Manning was here in order to prepare himself for Popovic testimony, there were some information missing from the field, and that's why I went on a mission to get the information he needed for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. I will not dwell on this any further, but let me ask you this: Can you tell us what the difference is between the International Commission on Missing Persons and the Institute for Missing Persons? And tell us the difference between the acronyms of these two institutions, because you use them in your report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As you -- as you can see from the name of the ICMP, International Commission for Missing Persons, that is the commission established by the international community and also founded by the international community. And within Bosnia, there is also the Institution on Missing Persons which has been established by the BiH authorities. There were mainly -- before that, there were two commissions from the federation and RS side, and I think now they merged into the institute, and their involvement basically is to identify -- to find and to exhume all the additional graves which are found in the area of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, those related to Srebrenica and also those related to other incidents. And the basic distinction between those two is that one is the government organisation institution and the other one is international institution which one day will disappear from Bosnia, but the government institute will remain there and it will continue with its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. You are talking here about a government institution. But in order to be absolutely certain, because we use these documents in preparation for our Defence and the Court, can you please tell us who established that commission or that institute, the federal commission or institute, and which government is its founder? Is it the Bosnian government or the federal government, because you also mentioned Republika Srpska now, so -- and it's all confusing, so could you please tell us who is the source for these documents and whom can we ask for documents from?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up until, I think, 2008, there were two commissions inside Bosnia, the Federal Commission on Missing Persons and the RS Commission on Missing Persons, and those were established by federal authorities and, on the other side, by the RS authorities. And now there is an institute from 2008 onwards which I think merged both commissions into one institute, and this was established by the BiH authorities. But, again, I would need to get more precise documents on that in order to answer your question. So that's my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any documents from this institute? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, from the commission before and also from the institute, I received some documents, yes. And I also used some documents for my report, especially related to the surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that Republika Srpska and the federation differ on their views about this institute, and that they are currently discussing this issue, these two governments within the republic and the federation?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So, yes, it's possible, but I don't have this information. I'm not aware of this information, but it's quite possible as a normal thing in Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have no information on it, do you have any information about whether the OTP received any information or data from the International Commission for the entire territory of Bosnia, and then classifies that information within the OTP, or do you just receive information that have to do with Srebrenica in July of 1995, in view of the fact that that is the focus of the OTP's work? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OTP is getting, on a regular basis, both lists from the ICMP. When I mean "both lists," I mean, you know, the one which is related to Srebrenica only and the one which is related to all the other events. They have separated, within the institute, those two lists. And, yes, we are receiving all the data on a regular basis, every few months, from the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Janc. Could we now please show 1D125, and I would like to ask the witness some questions related to this document. Thank you. Thank you. We can see the preliminary list of victims of genocide in Srebrenica, 1995. That is what is stated here, and this has already been described as such before this Tribunal actually brought any of its decisions on it. Do you know whether this list was based on the basis of the ICMP and the government -- the federal government commission, and that it was published in 2005? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I assume there is no English translation yet. On your Defence list of potential exhibits, you indicated that the translation is still pending. Therefore, it could be necessary to read out what you are putting to the witness. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry for the delay. This document doesn't have any ERN number, and I wonder if Mr. Tolimir would be kind enough to identify the source of the information so that we can put this in context in terms of putting the questions to the witness. It's unclear what the source of it is, and I don't believe that there's a date that is actually indicated on it other than the reference to the events concerning Srebrenica. So if he could do that, I think that would be rather helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will ask the witness, first of all, whether he is familiar with this list and this title and whether he has this document as one of the documents in his possession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you deal with the comment of Mr. Vanderpuye. He asked for the ERN number and certain reference and the date of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that this was 1D125, and it was marked. It is a Defence document, and it can be found on the internet. It's an open-source document, and this federal commission is offering this document to all those who work with it. And this witness said that he is working with that commission, which is why I showed this document to him and asked him whether he has it in his possession. Thank you. And, Mr. Vanderpuye, I hope what I've said is sufficient for your purposes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you were referring to a 65 ter number. This is, indeed, on your list, but there is no ERN number yet. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, there is no ERN. That's a correct observation. The other issue is Mr. Tolimir hasn't indicated when this document was generated. It may be available, it may be an open-source document. It's unclear when it was actually generated for the first time. It's unclear under what circumstances it was generated. So the provenance of the document, I think, hasn't been established sufficiently to put questions to the witness concerning what it is, whether he has it, because there's not enough here to identify the document, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, if you are referring to the internet, you should indicate which web site you did take it from. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document was published in 2005 by the Federal Commission on Missing Persons, and we've also mentioned this document in our motion to this Trial Chamber. However, I can provide some additional information, or perhaps we can leave this document for some later time when we have its translation. But I can't really even follow the transcript because it's not being translated into B/C/S, and I cannot speak English and I don't have an interpreter of my own. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the reason why everything is interpreted to you in B/C/S, what is said in the courtroom. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My first question is this: This list, unlike the International Commission on Missing Persons, is a public document and available to anyone who wants it, and it lists information such as the first and last names, date and place of birth, compiled by the Federal Commission on Missing Persons. And on the lists are those persons who are considered by this commission as victims of genocides. And, additionally, it says, and that's on page 1, the preliminary list of the victims of genocide in Srebrenica contain information on 8.106 victims from whom it was established from independent sources that they went missing or were killed in and around Srebrenica in the summer of 1995. And my question for you, based on what I've just read out, is this: Can you explain to us why the list of the International Commission on Missing Persons, unlike this list of the Federal Commission, is not public? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of the ICMP -- the ICMP list is not public because of very obvious reasons, because there are the names of the identified individuals, all their personal details, and what is the most important why it is not public is because some of the relatives of those already identified by the ICMP have not been notified yet about their -- about their fate. So that's the main reason why, according to my knowledge, this list is not public.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Since that list is not public, could we move into private session so that we can actually compare these two lists. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we have only one document in B/C/S on the screen. There's no list yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we go into private session, because the witness just said that that information and those facts are not accessible and they have confidential? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now, the person whose documents we have shown - I'm not going to mention the name - that person was interviewed by the OTP in 2002. I'm not going to say by whom. I don't want to mention names.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I would like to ask the witness the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you explain to us how this comes about, how things like this can happen, and that somebody who has nothing to do with Srebrenica, but somebody who is from Zepa, crosses over to Serbia, and then from Serbia goes to the United States, that that person should be on a list compiled by the Federal Commission for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina, with which you are in contact, as we understand it from your testimony here, and it's also a witness of the institution that you are testifying for as an investigator? Thank you. So how come he's on that list?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First, I would like to say that I don't know, actually, what this list on the left-hand side represents, so I assume this is a kind of list from somewhere because I am -- I'm sure this is not the ICMP list, because it doesn't look like that. And if -- the only possible source which I see reliable would be the ICRC list, but even in that case I don't think this is taken out from the ICRC list. And, yes, as I explained before, the ICRC lists were updated regularly, and in case the individuals were found later to be still alive, they were taken off the list. And I'm not sure if this particular individual is still on the list. We would have to take a look into the recent ICRC list. And what I can assure, this person is not on the ICMP list as the one being found in the grave and the one which would represent one individual of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When I displayed this list, I said it was from the Federal (redacted) (redacted) Now, later on I showed you his provisional travel documents, and I said that that was compiled by the Tribunal and that he is listed as a missing person. How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say we did not refer -- I haven't completed my report based on the -- on this list, and it is quite possible that this individual, it is on the list of the Federal Commission on Missing Person, which for our purposes is not the reliable one. So the most reliable one would be the ICRC list, and I would like to check the ICRC list, the latest updated version of it, where this individual will most probably not be there anymore. So that's why we cannot -- I cannot comment on this list, because that's the list I have never referred to in my report. So what is relevant for my report is that this individual is not identified, and, on the other hand, we can see he's still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wanted to object to the question, and the reason for that is that, as we can see from the beginning of this -- at the beginning of this document, it's referred to as a preliminary list. And Mr. Tolimir was kind enough to read the first paragraph of the list, but didn't read the following paragraphs of the list. I can't read them because they are not in a language that I can read, but I think it would be helpful and appropriate to read in the rest of the preliminary page, the first page of this document, so that the Trial Chamber can understand the context under which this list was developed, specifically because Mr. Tolimir is now asking why a certain anomaly -- or how a certain anomaly on the list can be explained, and I think that can be explained by reference to the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Tolimir, could you help Mr. Vanderpuye and the Chamber with the information requested?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, for getting up, but I'd just like to say that I noticed, on line -- on page 25, line 15, since a number was mentioned from this list, to avoid having the person identified, I'd like that line redacted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this advice, but still we are in a very strange position. You indicated that you got this list from the internet. If that is true, then there is no reason for any redaction. Mr. Janc, the witness, told us why he didn't publish -- or why the ICMP didn't publish their lists yet, but there might be a difference. If that information is available on the internet, if that is true, then there's no reason for a redaction. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I didn't say "because of this fact in the list." The list is accessible to everybody. But in the context of the discussions we had, an individual was mentioned who's a protected witness, I believe, at this Tribunal, so that's the reason why I insisted -- well, I didn't insist, but I thought that it was a good idea to redact that line 15 on page 25. That was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. It will be done. Mr. Tolimir, could you help Mr. Vanderpuye and the Chamber with this request?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, I can, and I'll read out the whole of the first page, which is what Mr. Vanderpuye asked me to do. This is what it says: "Preliminary list of victims --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps not the whole page, but the portion Mr. Vanderpuye wanted to hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A preliminary list, it's not a final list, and will only be used as a starting basis for compiling a final list of the victims of genocide in Srebrenica. And, furthermore, it says who compiled the list, and what telephones can be contacted -- what the telephone numbers are of the commission, and they provide their address, their internet address, at the end of the page. And we can see that it's accessible to everyone. And as it was a list that was public published, I assume that they provided it to this Tribunal, because this Tribunal is bandying about a figure of 8.000-odd victims, so I would like to say that a number of people on those -- on that list are living persons, people who are still alive of those 8.106 on the list. Now, if I can explain further, I'd be happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where the internet address is? I don't see any. There are two e-mail addresses, but not the web site address. Could you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It says information can be given orally or in writing and sent to the Federal Commission for Missing Persons in Sarajevo, Musala Street number 9, by telephone, by telefax, by e-mail, with the e-mail address, or the association of the movement of the mothers of the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa can be contacted. And the address there is Trsnica Entar [phoen], Antuna Hangija [phoen] number 1, and an e-mail address for the association, which is "srebrenicazena@," et cetera, dot com, "epm.pa."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir, but that means nothing. You said it is available on the internet. These are normal post addresses and e-mail addresses. Somebody can get in contact with them and ask for that list, if I understand correctly, but there is no web site. So it is not, from the first view, available on the web site. Could you give such a reference? If there is nothing, if you don't have it, then tell us. And please say when this list was published.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This list was published in 2005, and we wrote about it in our brief. We indicated those illogical situations. And my question to this witness is the following: Did he ever check out the list provided by the Commission for Missing Persons of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and did he compare it to other lists of missing persons or persons killed? Thank you. Could he answer that question, please, if he can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not, personally. And if this was done, that was done by the Demographic Unit. But as I have already explained, this is additional source of information on the missing person -- persons from Srebrenica, and what was the most reliable source, I will explain once more, was the ICRC list and, for my report, the ICMP list. So we haven't used this list as being one source for my report, especially because this is, I would say, outdated. It is created in 2005, so -- and I'm quite sure that a lot of updates have occurred during these years, and the information which are available now would be, for sure, much different.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked you this: Did you ever check out the Federal Commission's lists? And they provided their address and everything. Did you compare them and check them with the International Commission's list of missing persons, and do you know anything about their lists at all? Do you use their lists in your work as a database of any kind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I personally haven't checked these lists, but it's possible they were checked by the Demographic Unit. So in order to get into the reliability and validity of data, you need much more information on the methodology and everything, how that second list was compiled, so -- and that -- that's what has been the ongoing process of the OTP Demographic Unit, and they will present their report on the actual number on missing persons in relation to Srebrenica. And I think they will also be able to respond on this question, if they have compared this list against any other -- any other lists. But for my report, no, I haven't used this list as a source. The main source was the ICMP list of the identified individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. So am I right in saying that most probably, according to what you've just said, the Demographic Department of the OTP used it for their purposes; yes or no? Is that right? Did the Demographic Unit check out the list provided by the federation or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible they did. I don't know for the fact, because they have checked many of those lists, and I think they can respond to this question more accurately than I can do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Well, in that case, I'd like to tender page 1 and -- 119 of 1D125, as well as document 1D126, where we can see that that particular person is alive, whereas he's listed as missing. Thank you. I'd like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification on two reasons. Firstly, there is no English translation available yet. The second reason is that this witness was not able to answer the question about the authenticity and the content of this list. Please carry on. Just a moment. The number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 1D125 will be D43, marked for identification, while 65 ter 1D126 will be Exhibit D44, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 30, line 12 to 13, of your evidence just now, you have stated that: "The main source for my report was the ICMP list." Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you able to say whether, from the latest report of the ICMP list, you could identify this person who has been discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to check the -- this information electronically. It's possible to check it very quickly. But I'm quite sure this person would not be on that list. But from the top of my head, I cannot say, because it needs to be done in an electronic way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: How long would that take?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can do it during the break, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Just before I let you go: When was -- the last updated ICMP and ICRC report that you used, when were those lists established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received the latest ICMP list in February, but includes all the identifications which were made up to the end of November 2009. And the latest ICRC list, I think it is also around February this year, but this information I will also need to check. But they are around the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness this, so that we can round off this set of questions: Under whose supervision did the Federal Commission for Missing Persons for Bosnia-Herzegovina, under whose supervision it is? Who controls its work? That is a question I asked earlier on, but I would like to have the answer recorded in the transcript because it wasn't previously. So who supervises the work of the commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this commission does not exist anymore, so now it's an institute. But before that, it was part of the BiH federal government, so -- and if you want the name of the individual who was the head of that commission, I can provide you with that also, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me why the name of that person exists, whereas the name of the commission doesn't -- as the commission doesn't exist?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What do you mean, that the name of that commission exists? Where does it exist? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you said that the commission no longer exists, so can you tell me the name of the person who headed the organisation that controlled this? How can it control something that doesn't exist? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the head of this commission, a commission which does not exist anymore from 2008, was Mr. Amor Masovic, and I think he's still the head of the now institute or the head -- I might be wrong with that, because it might be that there is a bench of the people who is heading the institute now, but he's one of them, for sure, there still.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell me whether he was the president of this Federal Commission previously or not.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So they are the same people; it's just the names that have been changed. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, not only the name, but, indeed, there are still the same people, and I already testified that they merged with the RS commission together into one institute, and most probably the same people work for this institute now, or at least some of those people are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now show us a document -- or, rather, I'd like to call up P2508, page 15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the number. It can't be the right one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to call up on e-court P208, page 15. P208. Thank you. Thank you. Yes, we have it up on our screens now. Now, there are 16 maps -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, there are 16 maps that you showed us when you were here last, and on every one it says "surface graves, victims of 1995." I assume that you received that from the institute in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, what organisation compiled these maps? That's my question to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That institute you just referred to, that was the Institute on Missing Persons, the BiH Institute on Missing Persons, and we asked Mr. Masovic for this map to be compiled and provided to us, based on the information and data they have already provided already before in relation to surface remains collected in this area between 1996 and 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in that organisation, the one that compiled this, does it have data on the movement of the columns, the way in which the column was broken through, the victims that were found, the combat -- those who were killed in action, and so on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand the question, but I will explain a little bit. So I don't -- I don't know if they have this information on this data there, but what these represent here, what we have in front of us, is -- are just -- are the surface remains which were collected in 1996, and the dots are -- the dots are showing the exact location where those located -- were collected from the ground. That is the purpose for this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Do they already speak of this in the title, itself, where they say how these data are to be interpreted? They say, in their title, as I read out earlier, "Genocide victims of 1995," whereas we see that these were combat victims who were left on the surface along the access of movement of this column; the bodies were found in the woods and other areas, et cetera. And you, yourself, said these were surface remains found on surface sites, that these were remains of people who were killed in action. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we asked them to compile such a list -- such -- this map for us, and the purpose of this was just to find out where the certain locations are. We did not interrupt with how they have made these maps. We just wanted to get the exact locations of these places. So how they have created them and what they have put on the document, it was irrelevant to us, I mean, in relation what is written there. So how do they title this document, it's up to them. But for our purposes, the main purpose was to find the location -- locations where those remains were collected. And I testified about what -- about what is our view -- my view on these surface remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Can you tell us, please, why -- when you present these maps, why you didn't translate what is stated on them into English, and the way that you would mark these maps, why is it necessary to get the maps but also the comments and attitudes taken by this commission on these documents that you are now presenting to this Trial Chamber? Can this be viewed as a sort of provocation or is this the regular procedure and how it should be done?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a -- it's not any provocation, but, you know, it's a document we received from them, and we just disclose it to you in its entirety, as it was received. So for the purposes of my testimony, of my report, only these dots we can see here are important, and, of course, also the information -- for example, on this page, we can see that, for example, a yellow dot, it means that it is 1996 related. So what is important for me were just these dots where these surface remains were found, and that was -- that's it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Janc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are already over time. I think we need a break. Would you agree with that, that this is a convenient time? Then we must have our first break now, and we adjourn and resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Mr. Janc was asked a question by Judge Nyambe with respect to determining whether or not this individual is on the ICMP list, and I wondered if it would be all right to provide him with a copy of the list and the ICRC list for him to verify and determine that information for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that proposal. With the leave of the Chamber, that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We resume 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, has Mr. Vanderpuye provided you with a document? If that is the case, you could now perhaps answer the question of Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually, I have made it, myself, in my office, and I've checked the ICMP list. This individual is not on that list. And I have also checked the OTP list from 2008, and he is not listed there. So it means that OTP does not count this individual as a Srebrenica victim, so he was excluded from the list. If he had appeared on any of those ICRC lists and any of those lists, he was excluded from those lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you may carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence has this ICMP list. However, it is in a format that does not allow us to search through it. We also have the list of the ICRC, which makes it possible for us to search it through that database, but the question is this:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is this ICMP list in a format that is not searchable? Is it possible to obtain it? Can I get it in a format that will allow us to search through it? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't see any problem. I think that the actual CD with all the data in electronic format has been disclosed to you. It's actually D0003272 and D0003294. You will find all information on those two CDs. I think they were disclosed in electronic format, and these are the ICMP lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, is it correct that -- no, it was just corrected on the transcript. Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In view of what the witness has just said, we will submit a motion for obtaining this document in searchable format. Could we now see 65 ter 2184, please, page 2, in e-court. This is the Dean Manning report from 2007 entitled "Forensic Evidence Resume on the Exhumation of Mass Graves in 2007." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Summary of Forensic Evidence on the Exhumation of Mass Graves in 2007."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 of this report, please, after we've seen page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You've said that your report relies on Dean Manning's report, am I correct, that it uses it as the underlying report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that it should be read in conjunction with his previous reports. It's not only one report, but several of them. One of those is -- as being this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may I read out -- quote the second paragraph in B/C/S that we see here, and it reads as follows, I quote: "Responsibility for the exhumation of the known Srebrenica-related mass graves sites was transferred from the ICTY to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2001. Agreement was reached with the government for an ICTY team to monitor the exhumation of some of these graves. Thereafter, Srebrenica-related exhumations have been undertaken by the BH government in co-operation with international non-government organisation, International Commission on Missing Persons (ICMP)." Could we now please see, again, OTP 65 ter -- I apologise. Could we see -- while we are waiting for that document, let me just ask you something about what I've just read out. Why does this document envisage supervision of the work undertaken by the BH government? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you would like to ask me. Why this document -- can you rephrase the question? I will try to -- try to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I will quote. It says here that: "Agreement was reached with the government for an ICTY team to monitor the exhumation of some of these graves." Why was there an agreement reached to monitor the exhumation of some of these graves? Why was there a need for such an agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to explain what I know about it, because in 2001 the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was not as today, and the ICTY was, up to that time, in charge -- in total charge of the exhumation of the graves in relation to the Srebrenica events. And in order to hand over all these ongoing activities, because we know that most of the secondary graves have been exhumed later on by the BiH authorities, and in order to hand over all these important duties to the BiH authorities, I think it was correct to make an agreement on the -- on the actual hand-over and also to make a kind of -- to make -- to put it down in writing that ICTY team can monitor these exhumations if in future would be needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. The last portion of the quoted section reads: "Thereafter, Srebrenica-related exhumations have been undertaken by the BH government in co-operation with the international non-governmental organisation, International Commission on Missing Persons." My question is this: Does this mean that the ICTY no longer monitors the exhumation and that the monitoring is only undertaken by the government commission and the non-governmental organisation of the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really. You will see in -- you can find inside this report, and also in my update, which of the secondary graves which were exhumed by the BiH authorities after 2001 have been monitored periodically or in its entirety by the members of the ICTY. For most of them, I would say up to 2005, they were periodically -- at least periodically visited by the ICTY. After that period, I think that we have not participated in these exhumations anymore. Those visits were, indeed, rarely. I have personally visited only one of such exhumation and only for two days, and that was Cancari Road 1. But for most of them which were exhumed between 2006 and 2009, ICTY did not monitor these exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Could you tell us, seeing that you went there yourself, what did the supervision or the monitoring by the ICTY consist of? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of my visit was not that much, I would say, in accordance to this agreement anymore, because I just explained that from 2005 or 2006 onwards, we have not been visiting these exhumations anymore. The purpose of my visit was a different one, not to be a superior to someone there or to monitor their work, but more to familiarise myself with the exhumation, itself, how it is going, and, of course, to see the actual secondary grave, what kind of evidence can be found in these graves, and to get an actual perspective of the grave-site, itself. So my mission there was not meant to be a monitoring mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. As you said just now, that as of 2005 the ICTY no longer monitors the work of the BH government commission or the ICMP, how reliable, then, is the data that you use here in this courtroom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are reliable because these exhumations were conducted by the BiH authorities in accordance to their criminal procedure codes, so each exhumation was attended by the investigative judge at the beginning, and then when they have changed the law, by the prosecutor. So the investigation -- the exhumation, itself, have been conducted by the prosecutor or investigative judge, and the exhumation report have been drafted by the official authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Apart from that, also the forensic experts have participated during these exhumations, and they have been collecting and obtaining and securing the evidence found inside the graves. Also, the ICMP have been presented -- have been present during the -- these exhumations with their archaeologists and also their other experts, and they have compiled the reports for each and every single exhumation. So my assessment is that information which are contained inside the reports which have been compiled after the exhumations by the official authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the ICMP are very reliable in order to use them for my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. We saw a few moments ago that the map with the surface graves, in other words, the surface remains, not graves but surface remains, were forwarded to you with the title "Victims of Genocide," although they, too, knew that these deaths occurred during the breakthrough. And here the OTP said, in the Pandurevic trial, that there were more losses during the breakthrough than in the entire Srebrenica event. Now, are we going to report this as victims of genocide or combat victims? What is your view on that, because you, too, classified them under the mass graves of victims of genocide in Srebrenica, and yet they were actually combat victims, victims of -- of those people who were killed in action? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a kind of combined question, but I will try to respond. When we are referring to surface remains, I think that I have made clear during my testimony that, indeed, what consists -- who are those individuals which were found on the surface are, indeed, the individuals which are -- which were killed in combat, and, besides that, also died during -- based on the -- because of the other reasons, not only the combat. But when I say combat casualties, and I testified that most of them is combat casualties, I still have a doubt that they are, indeed -- that most of them are combat casualties. Why? Because if you can see the area, the area where we have the concentration with the most of them identified so far in Pobudje area, we have almost 560 people so far identified and found there, so it means that many individuals have been killed somehow. On the other side, we don't have -- we don't have that many -- that many casualties on the VRS side during this period of time. So we know for some incidents where some of the members of the VRS and RS police have been killed in that area, but we don't have, actually, a lot of casualties on the VRS side. So the question for me here is, you know: Was it a real combat, when you have that many victims only on one side and on the other side you don't have -- you don't have much of them? On the other hand, when we see, on the Popovic segment of the trial video from the road, shooting from the armoured vehicles up to the hills, we can conclude that there was -- there was intention to kill everybody which is in that area, regardless of the fact if they were combat -- combatants or civilians. We know that part of this column were military personnel and also the civilians. And at that time when we see this shooting from the road up there to the hills, the VRS was at that time already aware by fact that part of this column are also the civilians, and we can see that information all from the same video, where you can see what is coming out of the woods. So there are old people, there are military-aged men, and, of course, there are -- there is one woman, and also we can see at least one kid. So when they have been shooting all over the places up to the hills, my impression is that their intention was -- the intention of VRS, to kill everybody who is there. So we have no real combat in that area. Different with Baljkovica area, where there we have a combat and we have statements of that, but when I am talking about the Pobudje area, where we have the most of the surface remains, I doubt that there was a real combat. So that's my view on it, but I will leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. In the penultimate sentence, you said "my impression was." Are you testifying here based on your impressions or based on forensic evidence, whether these people were killed as a result of hand-grenade blasts or shell fragments, and yet here you say that you are testifying on the basis of your impressions, but in the report you describe how a wound was incurred and you describe whether it was a gun-shot wound or something else? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, my expression was not the best one. Better would be that this is my conclusion, based on the facts that I have just been describing, based on the facts what is going on, what we do know from the documents we have, from the videos, from the statements, and other facts, so that is everything based on the facts. And my conclusion is what I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When asked by Mr. Mindua why you counted the surface remains as combat casualties or casualties as prisoners of war, you said that this was based on a witness statement. Now, is one witness statement enough to count the 187 surface remains as prisoners of war who had been shot after they had been captured, and yet they hadn't even been captured? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. One witness statement is, for sure, not enough, and I'm sure we have more than just one statement on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. But you were supposed to mention those statements and offer it here as evidence so that the Trial Chamber can judge on the basis of evidence, and yet we have not been disclosed any such statements -- witness statements by the Prosecution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we can provide those to you. For sure, we can find them, and we can provide them to you if they were not disclosed yet. But I'm sure that many of them have been disclosed already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. We'll come back to that question later on. Now, may we have displayed 65 ter 2184, page 3, please. May we have that called up on e-court. And for your information, it is Dean Manning's 2007 report. Here we have it, in English as well. You can look at both versions, and I'm going to quote. It says: "Previously, the ICTY relied on an anthropological assessment of the remains, known as MNI or Minimal Number of Individuals. The MNI was calculated on an anthropological examination of specific bones and was used, as many of the bodies have been fragmented during execution, initial burial and later reburial. The ICMP's DNA analysis of the human remains provides a much more accurate indication of the number of individuals located within the graves. The result of this DNA analysis are, therefore, used in preference to the previously-used anthropological MNI." That's the abbreviation, the minimal number of individuals. Now, my question to you is this: Can you explain to us in what way the MNI was previously determined, the remains of which are to be found in the mass graves, and to explain to us simply and briefly the methodology of establishing this minimum number of individuals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will try to do it, although I think the anthropologist would do it better than me. But I know because before it was impossible to -- based on the conditions of the body remains found within the graves, especially secondary graves, it was impossible -- or it was very hard to determine how many individuals is inside this grave, and then a certain methodology was established, anthropologically speaking, to define how many individuals might be -- might be found in a particular secondary or primary grave. So -- and in order not to exaggerate the number, the minimal number of individuals have been -- have been counted for or have been estimated to be -- I mean to say have been estimated for each grave. So that was done based on a certain methodology which we can all find in the anthropological reports from these grave-sites, and there is explanation of -- on the methodology, how they have come to a conclusion that a certain number of individual is buried at certain -- at certain grave-site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Can you tell the Trial Chamber now -- I just read this out previously. It was determined according to the MNI, and now it's determined according to missing persons on the list of the International Commission. Now, what is more exact, and should this Court make its judgement on the basis of a free assessment of the members of the commission, which are a non-governmental organisation, or should it base its judgement on the basis of the findings in the graves? How will the Trial Chamber be able to know the exact number? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A more exact and the most exact number so far is the DNA identification, for sure, because it's not easy to assemble together the individuals which are found in two or three different graves. And anthropologically speaking, it's much easier when you have -- when you have primary undisturbed grave to say -- to say and to conclude how many individuals is found in a certain grave. For example, in Cerska grave, and especially in Bisina grave, where there are primary graves, there are, anthropologically speaking, the exact number given of how many bodies is found inside these grave, but when you have secondary graves, and that primary graves were disturbed with heavy machine and then bodies taken to another location, you will have a lot of body parts, and it's impossible -- not impossible, but it's very hard to estimate how many individuals is found in each grave. So my conclusion would be and my answer to you, that the DNA identifications are the most -- the better -- the best source in order to come to conclusion how many individuals have been found in certain graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, can you explain to us, when it comes to this DNA establishing of facts and the minimum number, the MNI, and the anthropological examinations that you mentioned earlier on, what the difference is, and could you explain the samples, and the differences, and why it was decided that a non-governmental organisation should determine this rather than experts? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The DNA identification, as it was proved over the last several years, is the best source of identification.
