So when someone is identified in this -- through DNA in Bosnia, in relation to these graves, that identification is not completed yet, so also in that case the conclusions and DNA reports about identifications are sent by the ICMP to the -- back to the pathologist who is in charge to assemble the body parts of one individual together and to assess if this body is now complete, and then that this body can be returned back to the relatives. As far for the minimum number of individuals, there is a certain method, how to count particular individuals, so perhaps you select one bone which, for example, I think that they have taken a femur or something like that, and based on how many of these bones have been found in any of these graves, they have estimated how many individuals might be found there. So you have to just make a certain criteria upon which you will be -- make a conclusion how many individuals is found in a certain grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Just explain to us, please, those experts, the ones who are in the field, on the ground, and do they have the DNA, and if they are 10 people, can they just look for one person with the DNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand what you are asking me. If you can rephrase the question. Ten people -- no, can you rephrase a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. If I'm a missing person, and they have DNA information, the commission working on the ground, and establishes -- looks for -- finds the bones and compares the DNA, and there's nobody else with the same DNA except for me, and then they find people in 10 graves, can they say that 10 people are missing or just me, looking for the same people with the same DNA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of us -- each of us has its own DNA, I think, except for the twins, and even in that case I think they have slight differences, but -- so if they are looking for one particular individual, they will find that one. And if inside the same grave there is 10 individuals found, those 10 individuals will have different DNA profiles established later on. So it will be the same. Anthropologically speaking, there will be the 10 bodies. The reports will say 10 bodies, for example, found in this primary undisturbed grave, and later on there will be a confirmation through DNA that, indeed, 10 bodies is found there, and not only that, those 10 bodies will have their names -- will get their names. So that's the purpose of DNA, to find out, even if you know, exactly, that -- which five individuals or which ten individuals is inside one particular grave, you will always, through DNA analysis, then be able to identify each of them, so who is who. So that's the purpose of DNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, for me to understand, and for the Trial Chamber, tell me this: So DNA from my hand or leg or one bone or another one, is the DNA different depending on where you take it from, the DNA samples? Are they different on each bone? Is the DNA on each bone different? Have I understood that correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: DNA profile, which will be -- which will be established later on based on the analysis of all these body parts of the same -- of one individual will be the same from any part of your body.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is it simpler, then, for the person working to decide -- and digging up the bodies to decide who has the DNA or for the non-governmental organisation to decide, that is thousands of kilometres away from the site, itself? Which would be better? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ICMP is, I think, 100 kilometres away from this primary and secondary graves. It's in Sarajevo. And depends on how you start and -- and the process, what kind of process you have set up. In this case, there is an international commission for missing person who is doing this DNA analysis. As we all know, this analysis are quite expensive, and the ICMP is funded by different governments in order to get the fundings -- financial means in order to make this analysis, so that's a thing which I think will be very hardly done by the BiH authorities, itself, when I talk to them. So they are afraid, when the ICMP will conclude its work, that the identification process through DNA will be much slower than it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, can you explain to me and the Trial Chamber whether, then, of the number of people who are shown will depend the money that the International Commission allots to the Federal Commission in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Does it depend on the number of people, the amount of money?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I would not know the answer on this question. Actually, I don't know if it depends -- I don't know. You know, it's the question for the ICMP, itself. So -- but it's a lot of -- a lot of things are related to money nowadays, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We've just seen the biases of the Bosnian commission that shows all the victims as victims of a crime, without seeing whether they were killed in action or not, so could a member of the Trial Chamber be led astray that way too?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't -- I don't understand what you mean by that we have seen. By what we have seen these conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, a moment ago I showed a map provided to you by the commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the title was "Victims of Genocide." They didn't say "Victims Killed in Action." And you explained to the Trial Chamber that they were victims of genocide, and you did this on the basis of one piece of evidence and one testimony. You had said last time 87 surface victims, you placed them all in one grave with their remains, regardless of whether they were killed in action or not. So can a non-governmental organisation decide about something like that through a political decision, take a political decision in the matter?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'd like to hear the answer. Then Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain. I'm not putting everything in one box. As you can see from my report, first it is annex A of the victims which were found in grave -- in graves, mass graves, secondary graves, and other graves, so -- and those we count as the victims of crime. Then you have a section under annex B where you have surface remains section, and I have explained for many times for this -- for my testimony what I meant, what this number -- total number of 703 individuals found on the surface represent. So these are different type of the victims, but they are, indeed, all the victims of Srebrenica events. So they all left Srebrenica, all those people, after the fall of it in July 1995, and they were killed later on or died of different causes and reasons, so -- and that would be my answer. And so then it's -- the purpose of my report was to distinguish these two categories. And based on the facts I am presenting during my testimony and everything else, I'm leaving up to the Trial Chamber to decide are these victims which are found on the surface also victims of a genocide or not. But I explained my view, my conclusion on it, and I think it's -- that was the purpose of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'll be brief. I wanted to object to the question, because, first of all, I think the idea of putting a question to this witness about what is appropriate or inappropriate for a non-governmental organisation to base a decision on, whether it's political or otherwise, is completely beyond his competence and outside the scope of his direct examination. The second thing is that Mr. Tolimir has mis-characterised the record with respect to Mr. Janc's previous testimony as concerns individuals that he classified as victims of the crimes involving Srebrenica and Zepa, in terms of surface remains, and he gave a specific example of a number of individuals that were executed near Nezuk that's contained in the witness statement that I alerted the Trial Chamber to, that is the subject of a pending 92 bis motion application. That was -- I think it was PW-009. And that was the content in which that evidence came in, so I think it is inappropriate for Mr. Tolimir to characterise Mr. Janc's assessment or determination as to whether or not these murder victims are somehow a part of combat-related offences or combat-related killings, where there is clear evidence that indicates that they are murder victims and they are counted as such despite the fact that they're surface remains. And I think that Mr. Tolimir has mis-characterised that on a number of occasion, and that's why I wanted to bring it to attention of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, isn't it the case that these kinds of problems should be raised during re-examination? I mentioned that several times already. I think this witness is in a position to answer properly from his experience, his observations, and his knowledge, and it is quite clear to everybody that the questions Mr. Tolimir has put to the witness were formulated from a specific point of view of this accused. I think you should let the -- leave these questions for your re-examination at the end of the evidence of this witness. On the other hand, Mr. Tolimir, you should be careful the way you phrase your questions. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'd like to ask the witness to answer the following question: Whether the number of people who were later determined on the basis of DNA, when the establishment process was changed, was different from the number that was established through anthropological analysis, and if there is a difference, could he explain the cause of those differences? Thank you. The reason for those differences.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the individuals for the graves -- for the primary graves, undisturbed ones, I think that the estimate was quite exact and is still the same when we have the DNA identification -- identifications now. And for the secondary and primary disturbed graves, there is a difference in some -- in some sites. I don't know -- I cannot remember from the top of my head for which sites. We would have to look into the -- into the anthropological reports, but there is a difference, yes. There were, for example, much more -- not much more, but more or less individuals identified through the MNI process than we have them now identified through the DNA. So one of the reasons I have been talking about this already before, because we have the problem that one body -- body of one individual is in so many pieces that it is impossible sometimes to get the good estimate of how many bodies is inside a particular grave. And now when we have the DNA connections and -- DNA identifications, and based on the connections between the sites, we can see that that was, indeed, the case that so many body parts were found in two different graves of one individual. And one of the reasons why we have more or less individuals found or identified through DNA, then it is presented as an MNI number, is because simply that was a minimum number of individuals which can be found -- which was found in that grave or which is estimated for this particular grave. And now when we have DNA identification, of course, the exact number is coming out. And when we have the problem of half body being on one side and the other part inside the other grave, that's the problem then, because when the MNI have been counted, it's possible that this body or body parts, especially if you have the majority of the body in both graves, that this body was perhaps counted twice as an M -- as a minimum number of individuals. So that's my understanding of it, and that's why I say that was -- minimum number of individuals was an estimate which was sufficient enough at that time. But now when we have DNA identification, I would rely only -- mostly on DNA identifications because they are more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Could you tell me now and the Trial Chamber whether that means that a larger number of persons is shown than the real number, when that minimal number was used, and now when DNA is being used, that possibility has been excluded, and how could the Trial Chamber know what is correct and what is not? That's my first question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the minimal number of individuals, it is always an assessment of how many individuals is inside there, and I don't think that the numbers are that higher or different. We would need to take into a particular grave-site to see a difference, how many of them have been identified before and through DNA analysis now. So I don't see any big differences in these two, especially because, as I already explained several times, the DNA identification is more accurate. And even if we have slight differences between now and before, I would say for the Trial Chamber that a more correct number is, for sure, the DNA identification number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Janc, this: Is there the possibility now to determine the number of individuals on the basis of an assessment, as you said earlier on, or is it established on the basis of evidence and proof, because you said 10 persons? Why would you look for me in 10 different locations if you're just looking for me? So it's not 10 people, it's 10 parts, so why did you resort to that free assessment method when establishing the number of individuals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to answer it, although it's, again, not that clear a question. But in total, there is a certain number of individuals which are on the missing list, and during the process -- the identification process, there is intention to identify these individuals, regardless of the fact if a certain individual is found in 10 or 20 -- even 20 different pieces. So it will always come back to one individual. Even if the individual was found in that many pieces, DNA samples will show which of those pieces are part of one individual, and they will be assembled together. And the ICMP will match this DNA to the donors and then will have the actual identification made of -- on one body or on several body parts. So that's the process how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I do understand the method, but tell me, why was it necessary to change the methodology from the MNI to the DNA methodology? Did that actually bring, as a result, a change in the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not done in order to change these numbers, but it was done simply for the reason that we'll get the -- that we'll identify as many if not all of them, all the victims, which are on the missing list. So the best possible way to identify certain individuals is through DNA identification. And after so many years when those body parts and bodies have been buried in the area, because we know recently that -- some of them have been exhumed just recently and some of them will be exhumed in the future, the only possible way, after so many years, is to identify those individuals through DNA identifications. So I think that the other methods would be much less successful, and that's why they have changed in 2001 to start -- to a new methodology, so to DNA identification process. So -- and we can see how many have been achieved so far, so we see how many of them have been identified so far, and I think we are getting quite good results on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, whether, in the course of the sanitary -- sanitation of the battle-field, and related to the surface remains, whether there were any bodies that had actually been buried there before the events of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the -- based on the information we have, and I'm referring specifically to the statements of those involved, victims, then -- yes, involved from both sides, and especially based on the aerial images, when we can see exactly when those -- or roughly when those places -- locations have been disturbed, and when we have -- we don't have any documents or not sufficient documents or statements showing that these surface remains were, indeed, collected from the ground and buried in any other locations - I'm excepting here under Kravica and, actually, the Glogova, where we know that some other bodies have been collected along the road, which were on the surface and were buried there - based on all these facts I would exclude this possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Tell us, then, how did it come about, and you told us last time, that near Potocari a grave was found, a mixed grave where there were victims of 1992 and bodies of people killed in 1995, how was that possible unless there was a burial together of these surface remains and the victims or bodies of victims who had been killed earlier?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are referring to Bljeceva 1 grave-site, which I testified about that this is, indeed, a mixed grave consisting of the bodies and body parts related to different events, and this is the only -- the only grave or grave-site which is a mixed grave. So how it is possible that they contain those bodies from two different events, I don't know, actually, because -- but it is not that unlogical [sic], because most probably the victims from the 1992 events which are also inside this grave needed to be hidden somewhere, and because this grave-site, Bljeceva 1, is actually not that far away from Bratunac, they have most probably made a decision at that time that bodies will be disposed into a same secondary grave as victims from Glogova, from Srebrenica-related events. And, yes, they are actually not -- even if it is a mixed grave, you can conclude from the summary -- ICMP summary report that they were disposed inside separately, and first two deposits which are found out of seven inside this grave are related to Srebrenica, the other five deposits there are related to 1992 events. So that's my view on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. That is your view. Now, we had a witness here yesterday who, in 1992, was a member of the JNA in Vukovar, and he was tried before this Tribunal for Srebrenica victims. Now, could he be found responsible for the victims of 1992, although he hadn't even participated during -- in that combat, and also for the victims of 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he did not participate in such events, I don't see any reason why he would be responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But how will you make a distinction whether I, for instance, am responsible for one set of victims or another set of victims? I am being tried here, and their bodies parts are in the same grave and they are shown here on the table as victims of those events, how will there be a distinction between whether these victims were those of 1992 or those of 1995? And the second part of my question is: Did you actually interview the people --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last portion of his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, did you receive the request of the interpreters? You should repeat the last portion of your question. The record stopped with the words "did you actually interview the people," and then there's no record anymore. Please repeat from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you interview the OTP witnesses who came here to this Trial Chamber -- to this Court, and who conducted the sanitisation of the battle-field, and who collected the body parts of those individuals who were killed in 1995 and who are buried in the same mass grave where the 1992 victims were? And you said this was Bljeceva 1, and I'm saying that this is near Bratunac, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, because they will recall what you said earlier about this.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, okay, let me go first to your first part of the question, when you are asking me how is it possible that all the victims -- how to distinguish between 1992 and 1995. For the purposes -- for the purposes of my report, the victims from 1995 which are in Bljeceva 1 grave, the mixed secondary grave, are not included in my report, not counted as the victims from Srebrenica, and are excluded from my report. So in total, I think 49 people -- I'm counting 49 people have been identified from Bljeceva 1. Yes, 49 from Bljeceva 9 [sic] grave which are related to Srebrenica event -- events. And in addition, there is 91 individuals which are related to 1992 events, which are -- and those are not part of my report. So those are excluded, although we have information on who these people are and what incidents they were victims of. For the second one, yes, we did interview -- we did interview some sanitation personnel who was in charge to clean up -- to clean up the area, but they have been cleaning around Kravica warehouse, where the mass execution took place, then in Bratunac, Bratunac Vuk Karadzic school, around it, and in Bratunac, I think, Stadium, and then along the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road, and those individuals were identified and were interviewed, and also some of them testified here at this Tribunal. I cannot remember from the top of my head if those were the same people who removed the bodies from somewhere in Bratunac to Bljeceva 1, and I'm now referring to these 92 related victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to point out that we have an error, I think, in the transcript at page 60, line 14. There's a reference to Bljeceva 9, I think, and I think the witness might have intended something else. Perhaps that can be clarified. The other thing is that one of the statements that the witness was referring to, just for the Court's information, is PW-064, Witness 177, and I believe -- yes, I believe he's the subject of the 92 bis application, just so that you're aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Regarding the witnesses that Mr. Vanderpuye just mentioned, and we will discuss those witnesses on another occasion, but I would just like to say that we've heard Witness PW-009, who testified about the events near Nezuk, on the basis of which you estimated that all those people were victims of the Srebrenica events, and you did not make the surface remains distinction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, tell us, how many individuals are related to Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are referring to those identified ones, the total number of Srebrenica-related individuals is 6556 minus 15 of those found on the surface in relation to Zepa and 8 of those found in Vragolovi grave, which is also related to Zepa. So, yeah, this is the total number of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, a moment ago, when you saw that map, you said that you excluded all those victims but that you put them or relate them to those mass graves because of that witness's statement, and now you're telling us that you actually excluded or challenged 15 individuals out of this entire list of 6.556 individuals. And my question is: Is this realistic and is this something that you can determine realistically as an investigator, and whether this is something that the Trial Chamber should have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think these are the facts, that that many individuals have been found and identified so far, and they are all the victims. And I have already made a distinction between those found in graves and those found on surface, so -- but when I say the "victims," they could be the victims of a murder, victims of a combat, victims of a suicide, so those are the victims of Srebrenica. So those 15 which are related to Zepa events are, you know, just found on the surface around Zepa, and that's -- yes, that's -- that's a realistic number, because it is based on the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you interested in finding out when these victims were killed, whether this was during the events at issue here related to the July 1995 events or people who were victims later on, and why was your conclusion as it was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So for majority of them, we know when they were killed, because based on where they were found, they were found in mass graves, being primary or secondary graves, and it's, in total, 5.390 of them. Those -- for all of those, we for sure know when they were killed, because we know when those executions took place, based on many evidence, many documents, and everything else. And for the rest, it's also -- we cannot say for every each -- every each and single individual, when it was killed and when it died, but what we can say is when it was reported missing, so -- and as reported missing after the fall of Srebrenica and now found on a grave -- in a grave or on a surface together with other Srebrenica victims. We can reasonably conclude that these are Srebrenica-related victims. So -- but when exactly each and every individual is killed, I think it will not -- it will never be possible to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's a convenient time for the second break now. We have to adjourn and resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, continue. But first Judge Nyambe would like to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I thought I would just take an advantage of this pause to ask some questions without interrupting anyone's line of thought. The first question I have is: Is it your evidence that there are two methods of identifying victims, MNI and DNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, there were two methods in order to identify the individuals. So before the DNA identification, there was MNI identification method, and now we are relying only on DNA method. So what is included in my report is based on the DNA method.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Why was the change from MNI to DNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply because the DNA method is more accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Then what has happened to the identifications that were done before you switched to DNA, where you used only MNI?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to -- I have to clarify one thing, Your Honour. MNI method of identification, it's not identification where we will get the actual name of the individual, but this method relates to assess how many individuals -- unique individuals have been found in a particular grave. That is the difference between this method and the DNA method. With DNA, we get the actual identification of the particular individual with the name, so we have who was found there. With MNI method, we just get an estimate of how many individuals is in particular grave. So that for the purposes before the DNA identification, we have used this method in order to present what is the minimal number of individuals found in these graves, so not to present who -- what are the names of these individuals. So but with DNA methods, we get the actual names of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, your final list of identification is based on only DNA and not MNI?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct, only on the DNA connections. Apart from that, we have -- let me check how many, but we have -- we have 36 individuals which are also part of my report which were identified before through also -- by the ICMP and the ICRC, through also DNA -- through the anthropological means, including the DNA which was done at that time through ICRC and PHR. So I included those 36 individuals into my report, and those are individuals which are all part of the Dean Manning's previous reports, simply because they will be never re-identified through DNA by the ICMP because, in the meantime, their bodies have been already returned back to the relatives and buried. So -- but this is not -- this identification -- these 36 individuals does not relate to -- has nothing -- they have nothing to do with the MNI identification process. MNI is just to get the actual number of individuals inside the grave. If we are trying to make a full identification in order to get the name of the individual, we'll need DNA identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. Just one last one. What has happened, effectively, to the primary -- just a moment. What has happened, basically, to the exhumed graves? Have they been preserved or just exhumed and walk away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean they are exhumed -- for what period of time are you referring to, when we exhumed, when the ICTY exhumed them, or when they were re-exhumed by the BVRS [phoen] and the bodies were reburied? What is your question referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm referring to when you exhume for evidential purposes, have these graves been preserved, or grave-sites?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When those graves were exhumed and the bodies -- and the bodies found in them and all the evidence properly noted down and secured, the bodies were taken to the mortuary and also the evidence collected from these sites were secured. And after that, the actual graves were just back-filled with the soil, and nowadays on these places -- on some of them are, you know, the settlements, and these are normal places in this -- today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Okay. One last one. How do you distinguish -- and I'm specifically referring to surface remains. How do you distinguish from the surface remains which death occurred from combat or from execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's -- Your Honour, that's one thing which is not easy to distinguish, if not impossible at all, because in order to distinguish between those two, you would need much more information on each and every particular body collected from the ground. And I'm referring here -- I'm having in mind as these are autopsy records. As well as because when they are found after so many years, those surface remains have been exposed to the weather conditions and they are in bad preservation conditions. And in order to distinguish between those two, you would need more information, and the best possible way is to get -- to get the statements of the victim survivors and, of course, if you would have the possibility to look into every single autopsy record. We maybe have -- we may be able to say how many of them were actually killed in combat, but I'm afraid that this would take us -- this would -- took us a lot of time, and I'm afraid that it would not be possible, at the end, to say how many of them have been, indeed, killed in combat and how many of them have been executed. So it would be -- it would be very hard -- a very hard decision to take, so it's not easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue your questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Janc, you told us a little earlier what was possible and was not possible in answer to Judge Nyambe's questions. Now, can you tell us -- or, rather, can you answer this question, whether -- the estimate of the number of people killed in action, is this something that you come at based on your free assessment or based on some legitimate grounds which point to there having been some combat operations there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I concluded that on certain facts which I explained, I think, several times during my testimony already. We know -- we are all aware that there was combat -- there were combat activities and a fierce fight at Baljkovica region, and based on that, one can conclude that the bodies on the surface found in that area might be, indeed, related to combat activities. As for the other areas which are also part of my report, especially the Pobudje area, with the largest number of the individuals found there, I already made my conclusion before that it's -- we are considering them as combat casualties because that was the column which was passing, although I have explained my view on it and my conclusion based on the facts that although in combat, there are significant activities from the VRS which points at -- points at the conclusion that this was not a real combat, but just one-sided combat against the mass population, being the military or civilians ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Just answer briefly, please. Were these individuals, before they were killed, taken prisoner or were they actually combat casualties? Thank you. Please be brief in your answers, because we actually spend more time in your answers than on my questions.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure for most of them, they were not taken prisoners before they were killed, they were not taken prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go over the questions that I will have for you, and let's be brief. And for those questions where I seek no explanation, please give us as brief as possible an answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see Exhibit P167. This is a document from the International Commission on Missing Persons, transcript page 1777, lines 14 through 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye provided the following information, which I'm sure you're aware of. It hasn't come up on our screens yet. Mr. Vanderpuye said that this document should not be broadcast because it contains the names of persons whose family members do not know about their situation, or words to that effect. Now, my question is this: On this document, can you see the date when the DNA identification was conducted? And if so, could you show us the column where this DNA analysis is shown? We only see page 1 here. I'd like us to have a look at page 2 and 3. Pages 2 and 3, please, on Sanction. May I have the next page, please. Yes, here we have it. We can see it, but this should not be broadcast. Could we zoom in for the witness's benefit? He'll recognise it, because it's something that he presented. Can we see the date when the DNA analysis was conducted on this chart; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. The last column is the one you are referring to. This is the date, and I testified about it before that I'm not sure, but what I think is the date when the DNA report was generated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. Now, if we look at the person under number 1 on this page, we see that the ID was conducted in 2002, and now it's 2010. Now, why has the family not been informed about the identification conducted? That's my question, and a brief answer from you, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the brief answer is we don't see, from this information, if this particular individual -- if the family members were already informed or not. But I'm sure that not all of the individuals which we can see on this page, or on the following pages showing the same thing, that all of the individuals -- so we'll have only some of them which the family members were not informed yet. For most of them, the family members were informed already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see here that all the individuals have been identified from 2002 to 2004, looking at the dates there. That means more than six years have gone by since the time of identification. So why, then, are these persons listed on a confidential list still? Do you know that or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is based on the provider, so that was a condition of the ICMP, unfortunately, so -- and that's why we have to keep it confidential. It's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So the International Commission decides when you are going to inform that somebody has been identified or not; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, I don't know what is the process regarding the information of the families, but they are informing the pathologists, and the problem is that we have these secondary graves where a body part is in such a condition that it can be found in three different mass graves, and in order to put -- to assemble one individual together, you would need a lot of time, a lot of years, that it can be returned back to the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, I understand. Can you tell me whether the family should give their permission for identification in order to establish the identity beyond any doubt? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the relatives are informed about the identification, and they sign a kind of -- a statement. But regarding the exact process, I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there cases where the family did not accept identification on the basis of DNA? And if so, how many such cases were there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard about this situation, that the family members did not accept individuals as being their loved ones, but that is -- I don't know for how many of -- for how many such cases have been there. But I think there is a basic reason; because they don't want to face a reality that their loved ones are dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another set of questions now, and for that may we have D20 displayed, please. It is a report based on debriefing about Srebrenica, published in Assen in 1995 by the Dutch government. May we have page 38 pulled up on e-court, paragraph 348, and I'm going to quote from that paragraph. Thank you. Thank you. 3.58 is the last paragraph, 3.58, and I'm going to quote: "On Monday, the 10th of July, the commander of OP-M received orders from the C-Company commander to co-ordinate with the BH Army. That evening, fighting broke out among the BiH soldiers, resulting in dead and wounded. At around noon on Tuesday, the 11th of July, a number of shells struck the area near the armoured vehicle. The abandoned OP was also shelled. Chaos prevailed among the BH forces. Internal fighting broke out once again. That evening, the OP crew were permitted to leave because they were willing to take the wife and children of a local BiH leader with them. When the two BH soldiers with the anti-tank weapons attempted to prevent their departure, they were shot in the head by the BiH leader. This led once again to fighting between the BH soldiers." My question is this: First an explanation. Since you deal with the linking up of a mass grave with the locality where the person was killed, can you tell us whether you, or perhaps previously someone from the OTP, tried to establish what happened to the bodies of the Muslims who were killed in this specific mutual clash that took place in July?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that some of them were found on the surface, but for these particular ones, no, I have no idea what have happened to them, because we don't have any names and I'm not aware of any investigation being conducted in order to clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You don't know their names. Is it possible that they are in one of the graves and that you might have portrayed them as being victims killed by the Serb Army? Thank you. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everything is possible, and those would be the victims which were the victims of Srebrenica also, because we have -- if they are only surface remains, we have cases where there are suicides committed and also that there are -- that they were killed by themselves. We have such cases, and they were found on the surface, and they are part of my report as victims of Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are they counted among the total number of people for whom persons at this Tribunal are being held accountable and tried?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For these particular individuals, I don't know, because we don't know their names. But for the others where we have such a situation and we have their names, yes, they are included in total number. But not for the ones found in the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So in this case, you don't have the names, and you count them among the victims killed after having been captured and found in these graves; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, you're not right. So I cannot say that we counted them. So there is a possibility that they are found somewhere on the surface or somewhere and that they are counted there, but we don't know. From this information, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, can the Trial Chamber rule and judge only on the basis of cases that have been proved or on the basis of your report, which is a summary, for all victims, regardless of how they happened to become victims? So Srebrenica and Trnovo, that's 500 kilometres away from Srebrenica and closer to the safe area around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think we have explanation for most of them in my report, how they have been -- how they have died. Most of them were murdered, we know for sure. But for some of them, we'll never know. So there might be some individual cases, like we see it here, which will always be in doubt, but for most of them in my report, we can conclude that they were killed or executed. There is no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, the international forces here claim that a member of the BH Army killed two other BH Army members. I can't dwell on that any longer, but I'd like to show P170, attachment B to the forensic material compiled by this witness in April 2010. So annex B, please, or supplement B.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 60 of the Serbian and page 43 of the English called up on e-court, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch on your microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. May we have page 43. Yes, it's coming up, says my adviser.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, you refer to the DNA identification of surface remains, and now I'd like to read from the beginning: "In early 2008, the OTP received updated surface remains data from the BH Commission for Missing Persons pertaining to surface remains collected between 1996 and 2007, which are related to the events following the fall of the Srebrenica enclave in July of 1995." And in footnote 1, it says as follows: If you take a look at footnote 1, this is what it says: "This surface remains data is an update of the initial data. The only difference is the addition of 52 cases collected from the surface by the Finnish team in 1996, out of which 20 individuals had been identified as of the 28th of December, 2007." My question: In your report, does it say there - and just a brief answer - whether the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons conducted translation from -- does this apply to the Federal Commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whose list we had on our screens earlier on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it is a Federal Commission missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. These remains, do they relate to the Bare area, where the Finnish team of pathologists was working? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me for the Finnish part of it, the Finnish team collected those bodies in Kamenica area, which is the area behind the Kravica warehouse:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have displayed 1D100 next, please. It is the transcript from the Jean-Rene Ruez testimony in the Krstic trial. Ruez, as a witness, confirmed in his statement and during his testimony here well, said the following, and I'm going to read out the relevant portion on page 7 of the Serbian and English. So may we have page 7 in both language versions displayed, please, and I'm going to read an excerpt from that page. Thank you. And I quote what Mr. Ruez says: "This area has been processed in 1996 by a team of experts from Finland who were operating in that area in 1996, totally disconnected from our activities. They were collecting surface remains. But it's important to note that 600 bodies," and I emphasise 600 bodies, "have been collected in that area. These are bodies of victims killed in combat, in ambushes, in shelling, and possibly also in other circumstances which are impossible to sort out ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question: Mr. Janc, in your report you mention just 52 cases which the Finnish team collected from the surface remains in 1966 [as interpreted], and the main OTP investigator, Mr. Ruez, when he testified in the Krstic trial, says that the Finnish team collected 600 bodies. How do you explain that difference? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of this fact about Mr. Ruez's testimony, and I was trying to find information which was based for his statement, but I was not able to find it. And when we request the BH authorities, and I mean specifically the Federal Commission for Missing Persons, to provide us with a list of all the surface remains collected, they had provided us with a list of all the bodies collected by their side first. And as we can see -- as we have seen just before, that later they provided additional list because we requested, Please provide us also with a list of the individuals which were collected by the Finnish team, so -- and we can see from the list that they provided to us that 56 cases have been collected by Finnish team. In 1996, there were also other -- other bodies collected by the BiH authorities, and that might be the problem, because at that time, you know, that many bodies have been collected, but not all of them by Finnish team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I emphasised that this was from the Krstic trial, and Mr. Ruez, as the main investigator at that time, showed a film, but I can't dwell on that now. You say one thing, he said something else. Now, I want to ask you this: In footnote number 1 of annex B of your own report, you refer to the report which has an ERN number. It's a 65 ter OTP 120 -- so 2198, please, 65 ter 2198, page 1, to be displayed, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. This is a set of tables with the surface remains, and the total number in which you include the number uncovered by the Finnish team, and the total number is 877. Now, if we add to that the number that Ruez testifies about, 16, and the number of people whose body remains were collected from Bare, then the total number would be 1.477, am I right, if you add the two, put the two together?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you put the two together, you are right. But I'm afraid you cannot do that, you cannot put the two together. So -- and I think this is the real number, and I can explain, because of the identification we have so far -- based on the number of identifications we have from this area, how many bodies have been collected within these sites, so which might be a totally different number from number of cases which have been collected. So in total, 558 individuals have been identified from this site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now look at the first column, 1996. That's what we're talking about now. The number of bodies uncovered is 213, of which 163 were from surface remains recovery. That is a large number, and larger than 52. You don't mention the figure of 52 here at all, which you do mention in footnote number 1 from the Finnish team report. Now, when we have this figure of 52, how did the Finnish team collect 52 cases in 1996, whereas in your report you don't refer to those cases at all and you don't state this as a source of information that you used for compiling these tables? Can you now tell us what source you used -- what documents you used to compile these tables, because this number of 52 is not mentioned anywhere? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Can we scroll up at the top of this document? As you can see here, the ERN number of this document is X0189549, and this is mentioned in footnote number 1 of my report as being the table which we initially received. After that, we requested the BiH authorities that also the bodies which were collected by Finnish team should be included into this counting, and they have provided us with additional table, which is also part of my report, and I can give you the ERN. The ERN is X0189696. And if we open that table, we will find this Finnish -- this body -- body remains on that table. So I included everything and I considered every information I received from BiH authorities for my conclusions. So this is just the wrong -- the wrong table, because it's not here because they haven't provided us initially, but later on they provided it. And if you look into that other table, we'll find this 52 cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Now, tell me, did you ask the Finnish experts to provide you with the documents and the footage -- or, rather, since there is footage, did you ask them to provide you with the documents they used?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't asked them, and I don't have information on them, for the purposes of my report, in order to find out how many individuals have been found -- okay, or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where the body remains uncovered by the Finnish team in 1996 are buried? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am -- I'm still convinced that they are -- that they are part of the surface remains, they are considered as being collected from the surface. And if they were identified during the identification process, and most of them have been identified, they were returned back to the families and buried I don't know where; most probably, most of them in Potocari Memorial Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So your answer is that you don't know. Now, Mr. Janc, I have another set of questions I'd like you to answer. May we have Exhibit 170 displayed, please. Thank you. This exhibit was admitted as part of your report. It is not a summary of expert findings. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which exhibit; my report? I see my report on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm referring to Exhibit 170. Yes, that's the first page of it, that's right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, in that report, can you identify the portions, which are P170, which you personally arrived at and are not the summary -- a summary of the findings made by experts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand the question. But the report, itself, is in evidence, I think, and this is the summary of the reports, yes, made by the experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you indicate on this exhibit, P170, the report that you arrived at yourself, that you drafted yourself, and which do not actually constitute expert findings? Can you indicate those parts of the report that fall under that category?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are -- there are several parts of it in this report where I -- where I am referring to expert findings, to their reports. We can see it's actually part of the annex A. If you open the first page -- or the second page of annex A, you can see I'm referring to Dr. Haglund's report for Cerska site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. My question was this: Are there portions of this report that are yours alone, and also what are the portions of the reports that are findings of, let's say, the ICMP, or pathologists' reports, or other experts who prepared these reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- my report is combination of everything. There are conclusions, summaries, and also the findings based on the ICMP data. There is several information. The report, itself, it's not divided per section you are asking me now, but it's a kind of comprehensive report where you can see different parts of different sources inside the report. For example, for Cerska, you can see I'm referring to a specific expert's report where you can find more information on this particular site, and then below you have a table which is taken out of the ICMP data.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. Tell us, please, did you use the raw data, the experts' raw data, for your reports when you summed them up in table form, or did you, yourself, make that kind of decision?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What kind of decision you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, I mean this: Did you, from those other institutions that you just mentioned, receive data and then -- for instance, from the ICMP, did you then check whether that data is correct, or appropriate, or did you just take them at face value and insert them in your report without any checks, specifically in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you're referring to the ICMP data, we received this data -- this raw data, as you are calling them, from the ICMP, and then I analysed them. And I have used them in order to present them inside my report. And also during the analysing of these data, I have been evaluating these data. And as I have testified already before, in order to clarify any ambiguities inside the report, we have asked several times the ICMP for the clarifications. So we have been -- I have been evaluating the data, itself. I have just not used them and present here as -- as data, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "I" or "we," please tell me, do you mean just you, personally, or do you also refer to some other OTP staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to compile my report, I have been conducting analysis and I have been receiving support -- help from my analyst, Yota Vassou. And also in order to check this data with other sources, I mean ICRC and other sources, I have been in contact with the Demographic Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just sum up what you've just said? So you checked that information together with your analyst, Vassou, with an individual from the ICRC and with individuals from your Demographics Unit? Am I correct? Have I understood your answer correctly or not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with our analyst, we have made several different parts of it. I have put together the numbers of the identified individuals, but she was mostly deployed with the DNA connections in that section. And also we have been -- all the data which are provided to the OTP are received by our Demographic Unit, so the Demographic Unit is the actual first -- first unit which received these data from the ICMP, and, yes, they are evaluating this information.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please answer my next question. Did you review the autopsy reports together with a pathologist? Did you engage a pathologist on that work? Because you just said that you only reviewed them together with your analyst, Mr. Vassou, and ICRC representatives, who would be the most responsible institutions for cases like these for missing persons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the answer is no, because the actual ICMP data, they have nothing to do with the autopsy records. Autopsy records are something different which are important in order to establish different facts, and I'm reviewing these autopsy reports on my own, without any pathologist present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, that is what I wanted to hear from you. So you and Mr. Vassou, you assess these reports based on what you knew on your knowledge and your information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, if there is information we need to clarify, then I prepare an RFA to BH authorities in order to clarify a certain issue, or we send an e-mail to or consult the ICMP to clarify certain issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I have the answer I was expecting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see 1D79, page 3 of e-court? Thank you. We don't have it on our screens yet. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we wait for it to come up on our screens: We see here the objectives of exhumations -- in paragraph 9 in Dean Manning's statement, it is stated as follows, and I quote -- can you see paragraph 9 before you? "Some of the basic objectives of this project of exhumations in Srebrenica were the following: to confirm the stories of the victims and witnesses of massacres; to establish the exact number of victims; to establish the cause and time of death; to establish the identity of the victims and any relation with the missing persons from Srebrenica; to establish the gender of the victims; to establish any kind of relation or link between the primary and secondary mass graves; and to establish the connection with perpetrators." Now, my question would be the following --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you please repeat the question. The interpreters didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I was asking the witness to tell us whether these were also the objectives of exhumations and DNA analyses that are still conducted today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please answer the following question. Do you consider that destruction of evidence, items found in graves, would actually prevent a super analysis or super expert report that would -- in order to check the findings of OTP experts?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because if they are well preserved, and most of them are well preserved - we have photographs on them and we have descriptions, reports on them - then I don't think that would be necessarily the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Investigator Dean Manning mentioned, as one of the objectives of exhumations, as being that to establish the exact number of victims, and you say the same in the report that you presented here. You mention in several places the term "victims." Please tell us, was this a term you used mechanically for any individual whose remains were found in a mass grave, or did you have a specific definition for the term -- the exact number of victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is any specific definition for the term. "The victims" are, I think, the most common used in our reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Any individual who loses his or her life in times of war is a victim. However, in view of the fact that 7.000 victims are mentioned in the indictment against me, could you tell me, please, as an investigator, what is the number of those -- of that 7.000 victims, what is the number of those who had lost their life in combat and what is the number of those who had lost their life by an unlawful manner, in an unlawful manner?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that most of them have lost their lives in an unlawful manner. They were being executed, and I can say those found in the graves are within that category. And the ones who are found on a surface will be -- will -- for most of them, we'll not be able to determine what, indeed, happened to them, and we'll be considering them as combat witnesses -- combat victims. So -- but for most of them are executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Is that the reason why the number of victims in Bare was actually brought down from 600 to 52?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this has nothing to do with it. And the number was not -- was not taken down. It is just the matter of explanation, I would say, how it is possible. But as we have now the identifications, DNA identifications, we have been able to say how many of them have been identified and found on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Janc. On page 1743 of the transcript, when the Prosecutor showed you a portion of your report and quoted it, and said the victims of Srebrenica and Zepa identified by DNA and other analysis, and he mentioned that you pointed out the number of 577, in your reply on page 1743, lines 14 through 16, you said, and I will quote your words: "This figure is the figure of identified victims found in mass graves relating to Srebrenica victims as well, and this was an initial figure. The figure now, the total number is 577 victims." Since you are an OTP member and also a victim [as interpreted] in the proceedings against me, can you please tell us what is this figure mentioned as 7.000 victims mentioned in indictment in which I was charged, and what is the figure which is actually defined as identified victims? Could you please tell us what the difference is? You as a witness in this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN JANC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number which is on the transcript is wrong. It should be 5777. This refers to the victims which were found in graves. And the number 7.000 is the total -- would be the total number, I think, for the missing persons from Srebrenica. So in order to conclude the job to find the others which are still missing, there would be still some time needed, and I think, based on current calculations, there is around 1300 individuals which are still on missing list and are related to Srebrenica events. Others were already identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are really running out of time. You have indicated that you would need six hours for your cross-examination. I think today we had around four and a half or five hours of cross-examination. We have to continue that at a later stage, and then, of course, the Prosecution must have the opportunity for re-examination. Could you perhaps indicate how long the remainder of your cross-examination will be? Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have over 50 questions. I will need at least three hours, if you allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is really much more than the double amount of time you indicated earlier. In any case, we have to adjourn now, and I propose that the parties should liaise on the question when this witness, which is really a witness and not a victim, as we saw it on the transcript earlier - I hope you don't feel like a victim of these proceedings, Mr. Janc - you should liaise about the question which will be the appropriate time to call this witness again. Thank you. We have to adjourn, and we resume on the 27th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 27th day of May, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.05 p.m.,
